title: What Poetry Does
description: Compression, rhythm, image — what verse achieves that prose can't

concepts.title: Verse as Heightened Speech
concepts.contentHtml:
Every culture that has writing also has poetry — usually before it has prose. Poetry isn't a refinement of ordinary language; it's older than ordinary writing.

What sets it apart? Compression and arrangement. A poem squeezes more meaning into fewer words and arranges those words so that how they sound is part of what they mean.

Prose carries information; poetry carries information plus the experience of language itself. A novel describes the death of a child. A poem makes you feel the silence afterwards.

concepts.title: Sound and Sense
concepts.contentHtml:
Poets work with two simultaneous channels: meaning and music. The two are not separable in good poems.

Pope's line — 'The sound must seem an echo to the sense' — captures the principle. When Tennyson writes 'The murmuring of innumerable bees,' the soft m's and r's enact what they describe. When Hopkins writes 'shook foil,' the words flash like the metal they name.

This is why poetry resists translation more than prose. The sense survives a language change; the sound usually doesn't.

concepts.title: The Line as Unit
concepts.contentHtml:
The basic unit of prose is the sentence. The basic unit of poetry is the line.

Lines control pace. They create pauses where sentences don't, suspense where syntax wouldn't. They let a poet break thought against form, deciding moment by moment whether to flow or to halt.

This is why poetry on the page looks different from prose. Those line breaks aren't decoration — they're a second grammar working alongside the first.

concepts.title: What Poetry Is For
concepts.contentHtml:
Different cultures have given different answers.

For Homer's Greeks, poetry preserved the heroic past. For the Hebrew prophets, it was the medium of divine speech. For Roman elegists, it courted lovers and lamented loss. For Tang dynasty Chinese, it was a way to be a serious public person. For the Romantics, it expressed the individual soul. For the Modernists, it remade perception itself.

The constant: poetry is the form humans turn to when ordinary speech feels insufficient. Births, deaths, weddings, war, ecstatic religious experience, political crisis, falling in love. The big moments demand a different rhythm.

concepts.title: Reading a Poem
concepts.contentHtml:
Most readers approach a poem and ask 'what does it mean?' This is the wrong first question.

The first question is: 'what does it do?' How does it move? What sounds and rhythms does it set up and break? Where does it speed up, slow down, surprise?

Meaning emerges from those movements. Rushing to a paraphrase — 'this poem is about loss' — typically destroys the very thing the poem is trying to communicate.

Read aloud. Read more than once. Notice line breaks. The rest follows.

title: Meter & Rhythm
description: Iambic, trochaic, dactylic — feet, lines, scansion

concepts.title: Stress and the Foot
concepts.contentHtml:
English is a stress-timed language: certain syllables carry more weight than others. 'a-BOUT,' 'TA-ble,' 'in-fi-NI-ty.' Native speakers do this without thinking.

Metrical poetry organizes those stresses into patterns. The basic unit is the foot — typically two or three syllables with a fixed stress pattern.

An iamb is unstressed-stressed (da-DUM): 'a-BOUT.' A trochee is stressed-unstressed (DUM-da): 'TA-ble.' These are the workhorses of English verse.

concepts.title: Iambic Pentameter
concepts.contentHtml:
The dominant meter in English poetry from Chaucer through Frost: iambic pentameter. Five iambs per line. Ten syllables, alternating unstressed-stressed.

Shakespeare: 'Shall I com-PARE thee TO a SUM-mer's DAY?'

Why this meter? Probably because it matches the natural cadence of spoken English. Pentameter is long enough for complex thought, short enough to grasp at once. It gives sentences room to breathe but doesn't sprawl.

Drama, epic, sonnets, narrative poems — all gravitated toward it for centuries.

concepts.title: Other Meters
concepts.contentHtml:
Beyond iambs:

Trochaic: stressed-unstressed. Driving, percussive. 'Tyger! Tyger! burning bright' (Blake). Often used for chants and incantations.

Anapestic: unstressed-unstressed-stressed (da-da-DUM). Galloping, fast. ''Twas the NIGHT before CHRIST-mas.' Light verse and ballads love this.

Dactylic: stressed-unstressed-unstressed (DUM-da-da). The opposite swing. Used in classical hexameter; rare in English outside Longfellow.

Spondee: two stressed in a row. Slows the line; creates emphasis. 'Break, break, break' (Tennyson).

concepts.title: Variation Against the Pattern
concepts.contentHtml:
A purely metrical poem — every foot identical — would be unbearable. The interesting work happens in the variations against the pattern.

A skilled poet sets up an iambic expectation, then breaks it deliberately. Substituting a trochee at the start of a line creates urgency. A spondee in mid-line slams the brakes. An extra unstressed syllable produces suspense, a feminine ending softens.

Reading well means hearing both the underlying pattern and the variations played against it. Pope: 'When Ajax strives some rock's vast weight to throw, / The line too labors, and the words move slow.' The line literally slows because of the meter.

concepts.title: Scansion
concepts.contentHtml:
Scansion is the art of marking metrical patterns. Use ˘ for unstressed and ´ for stressed.

'Shall(˘) I(´) com(˘)pare(´) thee(˘) to(´) a(˘) sum(´)mer's(˘) day(´)?'

Scansion isn't a recipe — different readers may stress slightly differently. Its value is in noticing: where the pattern locks in, where it loosens, where it breaks for effect.

Modern free verse (since Whitman) abandons strict meter for cadenced speech rhythms. But even free verse poets often have a metrical ear — the ghost of regularity haunts the freest line.

title: Forms
description: Sonnet, ode, villanelle, haiku, ghazal — fixed forms across traditions

concepts.title: The Sonnet
concepts.contentHtml:
14 lines, iambic pentameter, a fixed rhyme scheme. The sonnet is the most influential fixed form in European poetry.

Petrarchan (Italian): divided 8/6 — an octave and a sestet. Octave rhymes ABBAABBA, sestet typically CDECDE or CDCDCD. The structural break (the 'turn' or volta) falls between octave and sestet.

Shakespearean (English): three quatrains and a couplet. ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. The volta often comes at the couplet, which delivers a closing punch.

The form's genius is its compression. 14 lines is short enough to require selection, long enough to build an argument. Petrarch invented the love-sonnet sequence; Shakespeare turned it into the deepest exploration of male friendship and loss in English literature.

concepts.title: Villanelle, Sestina, Pantoum
concepts.contentHtml:
The harder fixed forms — those with extensive repetition.

Villanelle: 19 lines built from two repeating refrains and a single rhyme scheme. The most famous: Dylan Thomas's 'Do Not Go Gentle Into That Good Night.' The repetition produces obsessive intensity.

Sestina: 39 lines, six six-line stanzas plus a three-line envoi. Six end-words rotate through specified positions across the stanzas. Elizabeth Bishop's 'Sestina' is the modern touchstone.

Pantoum: Malay origin. Quatrains where lines 2 and 4 of each stanza become lines 1 and 3 of the next. The result: ideas keep returning, transformed by new contexts.

These forms force the poet into rhetorical situations they wouldn't otherwise enter. The constraint produces, paradoxically, original speech.

concepts.title: Ode and Elegy
concepts.contentHtml:
Looser forms, defined by occasion and mood.

Ode: a poem of celebration, often elaborate in structure. The Pindaric ode (after Pindar) has a triadic structure of strophe-antistrophe-epode. The Horatian ode is more meditative, in regular stanzas. Keats's odes — 'Ode on a Grecian Urn,' 'Ode to a Nightingale' — are the great English examples.

Elegy: a poem of mourning. Tennyson's 'In Memoriam' is a 133-section elegy for a dead friend. Whitman's 'When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd' mourns Lincoln. Auden's 'In Memory of W.B. Yeats' marks a poet's passing.

The ode rises; the elegy falls. Both depend on heightened occasion to justify their scale.

concepts.title: Haiku and Eastern Forms
concepts.contentHtml:
The Japanese tradition developed minimal forms with disciplined intensity.

Haiku: three lines of 5-7-5 syllables (in Japanese — English translations often relax this). Two images juxtaposed, suggesting a third meaning. Bashō: 'An old silent pond / A frog jumps into the pond — / Splash! Silence again.'

Tanka: 5 lines, 5-7-5-7-7 syllables. Older than haiku, more spacious.

Renga: linked verse — collaborative chains where one poet's stanza becomes the seed of another's.

These forms emphasize suggestion over statement. A haiku doesn't argue or describe; it places an image and lets meaning rise from the gap. They've been hugely influential on Western Modernist poetics.

concepts.title: The Ghazal
concepts.contentHtml:
An Arabic and Persian form, dating to 7th-century Arabia, perfected in Persian by Hafez and Rumi.

The ghazal consists of five or more couplets. Each couplet is autonomous in meaning, but all share a rhyme scheme and a closing refrain word. The form often ends with a couplet naming the poet ('takhallus').

The mood is typically of longing — for an absent beloved, for the divine, for an unreachable union. The disjunction between couplets feels modern; the form has been adopted in English by Agha Shahid Ali, who insisted on its strict form against looser imitations.

Ghazals show how a non-Western form can carry an entire emotional grammar — one that European traditions don't quite have an analog for.

title: Imagery & Figurative Language
description: Metaphor, simile, metonymy, the work of figures

concepts.title: The Image
concepts.contentHtml:
Pound's 1913 definition of an image: 'an intellectual and emotional complex in an instant of time.' What he meant: a successful poetic image carries thought and feeling simultaneously, fast.

Poetry traffics heavily in images — concrete sensory details that do the work abstract description couldn't. Williams: 'so much depends / upon // a red wheel / barrow.'

The wheelbarrow doesn't symbolize anything obvious. It just stands there, vivid, in a sentence that feels load-bearing precisely because nothing is explained. Image work.

concepts.title: Metaphor and Simile
concepts.contentHtml:
Two ways of saying one thing in terms of another.

Simile: uses 'like' or 'as.' 'My love is like a red, red rose.' The comparison is announced. The reader holds both terms apart, then together.

Metaphor: drops the comparison word. 'Love is a rose.' One thing becomes the other for the duration of the line.

Metaphor is more compressed and more aggressive — it forces identification rather than suggesting comparison. The best metaphors do work that no literal description could. Donne: 'Thy firmness makes my circle just, / And makes me end where I begun.' The lovers' souls as a compass — surprising, exact, irreplaceable.

concepts.title: Metonymy and Synecdoche
concepts.contentHtml:
Two more figures, less famous but constant.

Metonymy: substituting an associated term for the thing meant. 'The crown' for the monarchy. 'The pen is mightier than the sword' — pen for writing, sword for warfare.

Synecdoche: a part standing for the whole, or whole for part. 'All hands on deck' (hands for sailors). 'America won the war' (the country for its soldiers).

Both create compression by routing thought through a chosen detail. Metaphor moves between unlike things; metonymy and synecdoche move within a single domain. Both shape ordinary speech as much as poetry — a fact poets have always exploited.

concepts.title: Personification and Apostrophe
concepts.contentHtml:
Personification grants human qualities to non-human things. 'The wind whispers.' 'Death came knocking.' Common, sometimes clichéd, sometimes profound (Donne's 'Death, be not proud').

Apostrophe addresses absent or non-human things directly: a dead lover, an abstract concept, a bird, the wind. Keats addresses an urn: 'Thou still unravished bride of quietness.'

Both are ways of populating a poem with presences that wouldn't otherwise be there. Apostrophe is sometimes mocked in modern poetics ('O Wind!'), but it survives because the human impulse to talk to things — to the dead, to the absent, to the inanimate — survives.

concepts.title: When Figures Don't Decorate
concepts.contentHtml:
The bad lesson from school: figures of speech 'decorate' poems. The truth: in good poems, figures do real work that no plainer language could do.

When Eliot writes 'I have measured out my life with coffee spoons,' that's a metaphor. But it's also the only way to say what he's saying. Plainer prose ('my life feels small and routine') loses the absurdity, the precision, the implied passage of time.

Hopkins: 'The world is charged with the grandeur of God.' That charged isn't decoration; it's diagnosis. The world is electrified. The metaphor's strangeness is the point.

Test of a figure: try to translate it to flat prose. If the prose says everything the figure said, it was decoration. If the prose loses something irreplaceable, the figure was doing work.

title: Schools & Movements
description: Romantics, Modernists, Beats, New Formalism — poetics across eras

concepts.title: Romantic Poetry
concepts.contentHtml:
Late 18th to mid-19th century. Reaction against Enlightenment rationality.

Core values: feeling, nature, the imagination, the individual self, the sublime. Poems argue that emotion is a form of knowledge — sometimes the deepest form.

English Romantics:

First generation: Wordsworth (the everyday raised to vision), Coleridge (the supernatural, the philosophical fragment), Blake (mythic, prophetic).

Second generation: Byron (ironic, theatrical, sexually charged), Shelley (revolutionary, philosophical), Keats (sensuous, doomed, deeply influential on what came after).

Romantic poetics emphasized sincerity over rhetoric, organic over geometric form, the local over the cosmopolitan. Wordsworth's 'language really used by men' opened a door modern poetry has been walking through ever since.

concepts.title: Modernism
concepts.contentHtml:
Roughly 1910-1940. Sharp break with Romantic and Victorian inheritance.

Pound's slogan: 'Make it new.' The Modernists rejected smooth narrative, predictable forms, and direct sentiment. They wrote difficult poems with fractured surfaces and demanding allusions.

Key figures: T.S. Eliot ('The Waste Land,' 'Four Quartets'), Ezra Pound ('Cantos'), William Carlos Williams (American everyday), Wallace Stevens (philosophical), Marianne Moore (formal precision), H.D. (imagism), Hart Crane.

Hallmarks: collage, allusion, juxtaposition, free verse, urban subject matter, the mythic past haunting the modern moment, often a feeling of cultural exhaustion or fracture.

Whether you love or distrust Modernism, you're still operating in its wake. Most contemporary serious poetry inherits its formal and intellectual habits.

concepts.title: Postwar American Schools
concepts.contentHtml:
The mid-20th century US scene fragmented into competing poetics.

Confessional: Lowell, Plath, Sexton, Berryman. Personal pain, mental illness, family trauma made into urgent poems. Sometimes accused of self-indulgence; at its best, devastating.

Beat: Ginsberg ('Howl'), Kerouac, Corso. Long lines, prophetic stance, jazz rhythms, drug culture, anti-establishment.

Black Mountain / Projective Verse: Olson, Creeley, Duncan. The line as 'breath unit,' open form, attention to the page.

New York School: O'Hara, Ashbery, Schuyler. Urban, witty, conversational, surrealist.

Black Arts Movement: Baraka, Sanchez, Knight. Politically engaged, drawing on African American oral traditions.

The schools fought each other. Their rivalries produced more variety in mid-century American poetry than perhaps any other period.

concepts.title: Late 20th and 21st Century
concepts.contentHtml:
By the 1980s the school system had broken down. Several tendencies coexist now:

Language poetry: Bernstein, Hejinian, Silliman. Disrupted syntax, theory-conscious, anti-lyric.

New Formalism: Gioia, Hadas, Hecht. Return to meter and rhyme as serious tools.

Lyric tradition: Heaney, Glück (Nobel 2020), Strand, Olds. Personal voice, accessible surface, formal range.

Post-confessional / autobiographical: Bishop, Kim Addonizio, Sharon Olds.

Identity-engaged poetics: Rita Dove, Tracy K. Smith, Ocean Vuong, Claudia Rankine.

Spoken word / slam: a parallel oral tradition with its own venues and standards.

The pluralism is the situation. Pretending one school is the future is a sign of provincialism, not insight.

concepts.title: Beyond English
concepts.contentHtml:
The 20th century saw extraordinary poetry across languages.

Spanish: Neruda (Chile, Nobel 1971), Lorca (Spain), Vallejo (Peru), Paz (Mexico, Nobel 1990).

Russian: Akhmatova, Mandelstam, Tsvetaeva, Brodsky (Nobel 1987).

Polish: Miłosz (Nobel 1980), Szymborska (Nobel 1996), Herbert.

German: Rilke, Celan, Bachmann.

French: Apollinaire, Valéry, Char.

Caribbean: Walcott (Nobel 1992).

Persian: Forough Farrokhzad, Sohrab Sepehri.

Reading any of them in translation gives only a partial sense — but enough to feel the scale of what poetry has done in the past century outside English. Translation is the door; learning a language is the door opened.

title: Reading Poetry
description: Close reading, ambiguity, the experience of the poem

concepts.title: Slow Down
concepts.contentHtml:
Most readers read poems too fast. They scan as if reading prose, hit the end, and ask 'what was that about?' — the wrong question at the wrong speed.

Poems are written line by line, often word by word, with intense attention to placement. Reading them at prose speed misses what's there to find.

Practical advice: read every poem at least twice. The first read tells you the poem exists; the second is when it starts to do its work. Read aloud; this is mandatory, not optional. Even silently, sound the lines in your head.

concepts.title: Close Reading
concepts.contentHtml:
The technique pioneered by I.A. Richards, the New Critics, and modern teaching: close reading.

The method: pay sustained attention to the actual words, sounds, and structures of the poem, before drawing on biography or context. What is the meter doing? What patterns of rhyme, sound, image? Where does the syntax break or surprise?

Close reading isn't anti-context. It's about earning your context. You can connect Eliot to his religious crisis, but only after you've heard what 'Four Quartets' actually does on the page.

This was the great pedagogical revolution of mid-20th-century literary studies. Whatever your views on theory, close reading remains the basic discipline. Without it, criticism is just opinion.

concepts.title: Ambiguity Is Often a Feature
concepts.contentHtml:
William Empson's Seven Types of Ambiguity (1930) showed how good poems often work through layered, ambiguous meanings — not in spite of ambiguity but because of it.

When Shakespeare's Macbeth says 'tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow,' the repetition isn't a bug. The word's meaning shifts each time — promise, dread, exhaustion. A pinned-down paraphrase loses the layers.

Beginning readers want a poem to mean one thing. Skilled readers learn to hold multiple meanings at once and recognize when the holding-together is the meaning.

This is why 'getting' a poem is rarely a single moment. Good poems open further on each reading.

concepts.title: Don't Worship and Don't Dismiss
concepts.contentHtml:
Two mistakes in reading poetry, equal and opposite.

Worship: assume every famous poem must be brilliant. If you don't get it, the failure is yours. The result: forced enthusiasm, faked understanding, eventual abandonment of poetry.

Dismissal: 'I don't get it, therefore it's nonsense or pretension.' The reader closes off the genre that requires the most careful attention.

The middle path: many famous poems are great. Some are overrated. Some take time you don't yet have. A poem that doesn't work for you now may work in ten years. A poem you love now may seem thin later. Read for yourself, take notes on what hits, return to old poems with new eyes.

concepts.title: Building a Library in Your Head
concepts.contentHtml:
The deepest pleasure of poetry is having lines in your memory that surface when you need them.

Memorizing poems used to be standard schooling. The practice has fallen away — and most poetry teachers now think it shouldn't have.

Memorized poems behave differently from read ones. They become available to you in moments — at funerals, in love, in transit, alone in a kitchen. They're a resource you carry without thinking about it.

Start with what you love. A short Frost or Hopkins. A few of Shakespeare's sonnets. A Stevens. A Bishop. Two Yeatses. Half a dozen Dickinsons.

Twenty memorized poems is more than most well-read adults have. They will be there for you, unprompted, for the rest of your life.
